newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end sharply higher.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end sharply higher.

text.p: New York precious metals ended sharply higher as gold proved resilient enough to stave off further dips below $350.00, and physical demand coupled with comments from a leading fund helped to boost the white metals, traders said.
"In the last couple of trading days gold was unable to get much down past support at $350.00, and silver held its ground quite nicely," analyst Edward Kempf of the CPM group said.
"That's an indication that the troughs in these markets were reached mid-February and prices are having a hard time revisiting them," Kempf added.
COMEX April gold settled $3.20 firmer at $353.10 an ounce, traded $353.30 to $350.80. Later afternoon, bullion was quoted at $351.60/$352.10 an ounce by dealers.

Some traders drew comfort from Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer's comments on Monday that he had heard of no central banks planning gold sales since the Swiss announced their plan last week as a way of raising cash for a new Holocaust fund.
Tietmeyer made his comments following a regular monthly meeting of G-10 central bank governors, of which he is chairman.
Dealers said last week that the gold market's sentiment had been dented by the Swiss plan, coming from a country not expected to sell gold from its central reserves.
Silver reversed its initial losses to begin moving higher late morning. May COMEX silver settled 9.0 cents firmer at $5.275 an ounce, traded $5.30 to $5.16.
Volume in gold and silver was light at an estimated 28,000 and 15,000 lots respectively.

Palladium received an early fillip from an article in Barron's which quoted Julian Robertson, chief of the Tiger Management Co hedge fund, saying he was not tempted to sell of his hoard of palladium despite the big hike in prices.
Robertson said he remained bullish about palladium and suggested prices still had considerable scope on the upside.
John Brimelow of BV Capital Markets said a fairly serious supply disruption was developing in Japan, set to receive no palladium from Russia this year until April.
"The bottom line is that traders are short of the physical metal," Brimelow said.
Floor sources noted trade buying in platinum and palladium, an indication of a need for physical metal, traders said.
June NYMEX palladium went out $4.50 firmer at $155.25 an ounce, traded $155.90 to $150.75.
April platinum settled $5 higher at $383.50 an ounce, traded $383.50 to $379.50.
But volume was light, with only an estimated 518 lots in palladium and 1,337 lots in platinum.
"It appears that the equity markets in the U.S. have plateaued in the short-term and that is giving some encouragement to precious metals as well," CPM Group's Edward Kempf said.
